newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq given U.N. extensive missile data - minister.
newsitem.headline: Iraq given U.N. extensive missile data - minister.

text.p: Iraq has given U.N. arms envoy Rolf Ekeus data to prove it no longer has banned missiles in its arsenal, Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said on Friday.

"We have during the last visit given him (Ekeus) solid information, solid very extensive accounting of the Iraqi missiles," Rasheed, a former chairman of Iraq's Military Industrialisation Commission, told a news conference in Baghdad.
Ekeus, who left Iraq on Sunday, is chairman of the U.N. Special Commission disarming Iraq under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire.

Under the ceasefire, Iraq must scrap missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles) as well as all chemical arms, biological weapons and any potential to build a nuclear bomb if it wants international sanctions lifted.
Ekeus said Iraq had agreed to let him take scrapped missile engines out of the country for examination.
"We have every reason to believe that in the coming two weeks he (Ekeus) will acknowledge that Iraq has fulfilled its obligation in this major issue of the accounting of the missiles," he said.

Ekeus, a former Swedish diplomat and international disarmament expert, wants to know if the scrapped missile parts are from missing Soviet-made engines, as Iraq maintains, or from local equipment buried to divert attention from hidden missile engines.
Rasheed, who took part in Ekeus's discussions with Iraqi leaders, said there was a dispute during the meetings over accounting for the missiles.

He said Ekeus admitted in 1992 and 1995 that Iraq had provided proper accounting of its banned long-range missiles but had then asked for stricter and more extensive verification under American pressure.
"The basic fact is that Iraq has no mass destruction weapons whatsoever since many years now and the Security Council knows this very well," Rasheed said.
"But they say we want to verify it extensively under the American administration pressure because they say we have to go to the Security Council and they need proof," he said.
